title: Why have you forsaken me? (Mark 15:33–41)
hookLine: he cries the first line of Psalm 22, and a Roman soldier says: truly the Son of God; the women watch

cards: Some of the hardest words anyone says are said at a hospital bedside, at 3am, when no answer comes. Why? Where are you?
Mark doesn't soften what happens next. At the sixth hour, around noon, darkness covers the whole land until the ninth hour, about three in the afternoon. Then Jesus cries out with a loud voice.
Mark gives the words in Aramaic, then translates them. They are the only words from the cross that Mark records.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Those words weren't new: they're the opening line of Psalm 22.
The psalm starts in anguish: surrounded, mocked, bones out of joint, enemies dividing his garments. It ends in trust, the psalmist praising God in the great congregation.
Christians read the cry in different ways, and the readings sit together. Some hear real abandonment, the Son going all the way down into the silence people feel when God seems gone.

Others suggest that naming a psalm's first line can call up the whole psalm, so he may be praying all of Psalm 22, ending included. Some hold both. Either way, it matters that the prayer of the dying Jesus is a question.
Some bystanders say: he's calling Elijah! One runs to give him sour wine on a sponge. Then Jesus gives a loud cry and breathes his last.

teach.h: THE CURTAIN TORN, TOP TO BOTTOM.
teach.b: At that moment, Mark says, the curtain of the temple is torn in two, from top to bottom. And the Roman centurion standing facing him, the soldier in charge of the execution, says: "Truly this man was the Son of God."
Mark's gospel, in the King James text, opens by calling Jesus the Son of God. Now, at the cross, the one who says it out loud is not a disciple but a Roman soldier.
And watching from a distance: the women.

teach.h: TRULY THIS MAN WAS THE SON OF GOD.
teach.b: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, Salome, and many others who had followed him from Galilee. The disciples had fled. The women stayed.

how: Some churches hold a service on Good Friday afternoon, around the ninth hour, and some pray Psalm 22 or meditate on the last words of Jesus from all four Gospels.

o: a cry meaning it is finished, said as he died
Aramaic for my God, in Jesus's cry from the cross
a name for the prophet Elijah, in Aramaic

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: truly this man was the Son of God

s: Jesus's cry from the cross is the first line of a psalm
Psalm 22 begins my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
in Mark, Jesus speaks many sayings from the cross
in Mark there is only one: eloi, eloi, lama sabachthani.
at the cross, it's a disciple who says truly this man was the Son of God

games.q: you're one of the women who followed him from Galilee. the men have fled. he's dying. what do you do?
o: go home; there's nothing to be done.
games.why: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, Salome and many others watched from a distance. they stayed.

practice: If you can, open Psalm 22 in any Bible and read it slowly, all the way through, noticing where it's darkest and where it turns.
If you can't, sit with its first line, my God, my God, why, and think of someone asking that question right now. You don't need an answer for them; the women didn't have one either, they just stayed.

wordCard.voice: Eloi, Aramaic for my God, the first word of Jesus's cry from the cross. The opening line of Psalm 22, cried aloud in anguish and trust.

orig.note: Hebrew: Psalm 22:1, my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? Mark gives the Aramaic, eloi, eloi, lama sabachthani.

carryVoice: Your line: the women stayed. When words run out, staying can still say something. Until tomorrow.
